﴿Lā uqsimu bihādhā al-balad﴾ ("I do not swear by this city"). He means Makkah, by agreement. He swore by it to honor it, and the *lā* is extra (*zā'idah*).

The first is that the meaning is: you are *ḥāl* (dwelling) in this city, that is, residing in it, because the surah was revealed while the Prophet ﷺ was in Makkah.

The second is that *ḥill* means that your sanctity is violated (*tastaḥill ḥurmatuka*), and the disbelievers harm you, even though in Makkah it is not permitted to kill game, to kill a person, or to cut trees. The third is that *ḥill* means *ḥalāl* (permitted): what is permitted to you in this city is whatever you wish, including fighting the disbelievers and other things not permitted to anyone else. This is the most apparent view, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "This city is sacred; Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth. On that day the Messenger ﷺ ordered the killing of Ibn Khaṭal, who was clinging to the curtains of the Kaʿbah.

It has also been said that on this view the surah is Madinan, revealed on the day of the conquest, but this is weak.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 90, verses 5–7:

﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ On this there are two opinions. One is that its meaning is: Does he suppose that no one will be able to resurrect him and recompense him? The other is: Does he suppose that no one will be able to overcome him? According to the first, the verse was revealed concerning the category of the disbelieving human being; according to the second, it was revealed concerning a specific man, namely Abu al-Ashudd, a man of Quraysh who was extremely strong. It is also said it was ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd, who is the one who stormed the trench in Madinah and whom ʿAli ibn Abi Talib killed. ﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ That is, much. It is recited as lubadan with a damma and with a kasra on the lam, and it is the plural of lubdah (with damma or kasra), which means abundance. The verse was revealed, according to some, concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, for he spent wealth in an effort to corrupt the affair of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is also said it concerns al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal, who had embraced Islam and spent on charities and expiations, and then said, "I have squandered my wealth since I followed Muhammad." ﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ This may be a denial of his statement, "I have squandered wealth in abundance," or an indication that he spent it out of showing off (riyaʾ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 90, verse 10–16:

﴿وَهَدَيْنَاهُ ٱلنَّجْدَينِ﴾ "And We guided him to the two highways" – i.e., the two paths of good and evil. So it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3]. Guidance here does not mean direction (irshad). It was also said: it means the two breasts of the mother.

﴿فَلاَ ٱقتَحَمَ ٱلْعَقَبَةَ﴾ "But he has not attempted the ascent" – iqtihām (forcing one's way through, rushing in) is entering with force and hardship. "Al-'aqaba" (the steep ascent) is a metaphor for the righteous deeds mentioned afterwards, and it was called an "ascent" by way of metaphor from the steep ascent of a mountain, because it is difficult and its climbing is hard upon the souls. It was also said: it is a mountain in Hell, having a steep path which none crosses except those who perform these deeds. The particle "la" here is not for restriction (takhsis); it carries the sense of "hallā" (why did he not...). It was also said: it is a supplication (du'a'). It was also said: it is a negation particle. This view was objected to on the grounds that when the negative "la" enters a past-tense verb, its repetition is required. Al-Zamakhshari answered that it is repeated in meaning, and the sense is: "So he did not attempt the ascent, nor free a neck, nor feed a needy person." Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17] indicates repetition, since the sense is: "So he did not attempt the ascent, nor did he believe."

﴿وَمَآ أَدْرَاكَ مَا ٱلْعَقَبَةُ﴾ "And what can make you know what the ascent is?" – then He explained "the ascent" as "freeing a neck," which is emancipating it, and feeding.

It was read as "fakku raqabatin" with a damma on the kaf and the raqaba in the genitive (khafd), and on this reading it is an explanation of "al-'aqaba." It was also read with a fatha on the kaf and the raqaba in the accusative (nasb), and on this reading it is an explanation of "iqtahama." Fakk al-raqaba is freeing it (itq).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever frees a believing neck, Allah will free for every limb of his a limb of his from the Fire." A Bedouin said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Direct me to a deed by which I may be saved." He said: "Free the neck and emancipate the soul (nasama)." The Bedouin said: "Are these not one thing?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No. Emancipating the soul is that you alone free it, and freeing the neck is that you contribute to its price." As for ransoming Muslim captives from the hands of the disbelievers, it is greater in reward than manumission, because it is obligatory, even if the wealth of the Muslims is entirely consumed by it; but it does not count toward expiations (kaffarat) as freeing a neck does.

﴿أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ﴾ "Or feeding" – whoever reads "fakku" with a damma reads "it'am" in the nominative by coordination (ataf), a verbal noun upon a verbal noun. Whoever reads "fakka" with a fatha reads "aṭ'ama" with a fatha on the hamza and the mim, coordinating a verb upon a verb.

﴿فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ﴾ "On a day of hunger" – i.e., a day of famine. It is said: "sagiba al-rajul" when the man became hungry.

﴿يَتِيماً ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ﴾ "An orphan near of kin" – i.e., one having kinship; in this is the reward of feeding an orphan and maintaining the ties of kinship.

﴿أَوْ مِسْكِيناً ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ﴾ "Or a needy person in misery" – i.e., one in need. It is said: "taraba al-rajul" when the man became poor, and it is derived from "sadaqa bi-l-turab" (lying in the dust). It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he is the one whose shelter is the refuse heaps.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 90, verses 17–20:

﴿ثُمَّ كَانَ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُواْ﴾ [Then he was among those who believed]. Thumma (then) here indicates succession in rank, not in time, and in it there is an indication that faith is higher than freeing a slave and feeding others. It cannot be taken as sequence in time, because it does not follow that faith comes after freeing a slave and feeding others, and no deed is accepted except from a believer.

﴿وَتَوَاصَوْاْ بِٱلصَّبْرِ﴾ [and enjoined one another to patience]: they urged one another to be patient in accepting God's decree. It seems that this refers to the patience of the Muslims in Makkah in the face of the harm inflicted by the disbelievers.

﴿وَتَوَاصَوْاْ بِٱلْمَرْحَمَةِ﴾ [and enjoined one another to compassion]: that is, they urged one another to show mercy to the needy and others. It was also said: compassion (al-marhamah) is everything that leads to the mercy of God.

﴿ٱلْمَيْمَنَةِ﴾ [the companions of the right hand]: the direction of the right. ﴿ٱلْمَشْأَمَةِ﴾ [the companions of the left hand]: the direction of the left. It is narrated that al-Maymanah is on the right of the Throne, and it is possible that the two words refer to right and ill omen (al-shu'm).

﴿نَارٌ مُّؤْصَدَةٌ﴾ [a fire closed in upon them]: that is, sealed shut and locked. One says awsadtu al-bab when one shuts the door. The word has two forms: with the hamzah (u'sidat) and without the hamzah (wasadat).
